title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The preregistered estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms). We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Execution completed as planned: planned episodes = 480, completed = 480, hosted model call events = 240, model_calls_used = 240. Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm could create a discordant paired outcome only if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run every shared candidate passed validation and no repairs were invoked. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting and analysis, an artifact‑based failure analysis that explains the null paired outcome, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation from high‑level operator intent into concrete device configuration is a central objective for modern NetOps and AIOps. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can produce configuration sequences that are syntactically plausible, but textual or token‑level metrics alone do not capture ordering, dependency constraints, invariants, or transient safety properties required for safe application to live networks. Emulation‑grounded evaluation (closed‑loop testing where generated configurations are executed in device/simulator images and deterministically scored) has been proposed to surface these semantic failure modes [1].

A prevalent architectural response is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM generates a configuration candidate; a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants; and, if violations are detected, an automated repair step rewrites the candidate (or a human intervenes). Prior work demonstrates that GVR patterns can substantially reduce syntactic and many semantic faults in constrained settings, but open empirical questions remain: Does a deterministic verifier measurably reduce unsafe application rates under distribution shift and adversarial prompts? How should paired experimental semantics be chosen so that the guarded verifier can produce informative contrasts against an LLM‑only baseline?

To answer these questions under strict reproducibility constraints we designed and preregistered a paired experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) with a single, clearly specified primary estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline). Importantly, the registered execution semantics used shared_initial_candidate generation (one initial LLM sample per task reused across both arms). This semantics reduces model calls but makes verifier impact contingent on that single initial candidate failing validation or a repair being applied. The present paper reports the preregistered design, complete execution accounting, the artifact‑grounded analysis results, and an evidence‑based failure analysis that explains the observed null paired contrast and gives practical recommendations for future informative evaluations.

Research question and contributions. Our primary research question: Under shared_initial_candidate semantics and the declared experimental scope, does integrating a deterministic verifier into a GVR pipeline reduce unsafe configuration application relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired GVR experiment executed with an emulation‑grounded scoring oracle and declared model; (2) artifact‑grounded quantitative results and exact statistical outputs for the preregistered estimand; (3) a mechanistic failure analysis that explains a degenerate (null) paired outcome and concrete, artifact‑grounded design recommendations for future informative GVR studies.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents in network configuration have emerged to evaluate workflow and planning correctness rather than text similarity; NetConfArena is a recent example that emphasizes hidden executable tests and multi‑device workflows [1]. Prior systems research on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and demonstrates high repair coverage for certain classes of faults, while also noting limits on semantic coverage that depend on validator expressiveness [2], [4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as desirable patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety; they emphasize the value of closed‑loop verification and layered guardrails [3], [5]. The engineering evolution of model‑based configuration analysis tools such as Batfish underscores the practical benefits and challenges of verifier design and incremental verification in network contexts [6].

Unlike prior work that reports standalone system designs, benchmark proposals, or survey syntheses, our study combines: a preregistered estimand and sampling plan; shared_initial_candidate paired execution semantics; emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring; and complete archival of per‑call traces, verifier traces, and analysis outputs. This combination permits an exact, artifact‑traceable mapping from the preregistered estimand to the reported numerical outcomes and explains why, under the chosen generation semantics, the guarded arm may or may not produce informative discordant pairs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate, where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would produce a semantic safety violation when applied; safe_apply = 0 indicates no such violation. The preregistration specified a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms) and permitted the guarded arm up to one validator‑triggered repair per task.

Design, tasks, and sampling. The design is paired with exactly N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks. Tasks were composed deterministically into three strata: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks: novel topologies/vendors held out from task generation), and adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks: adversarial prompts created under a preregistered attacker seed protocol). The emulation test corpus contains explicitly encoded initial and expected final states and workflow constraints for each task; tasks were generated deterministically by the registered generator. The preregistration included explicit exclusion, retry, and missingness rules: infra failures could be retried up to two times and, if unrecoverable, would be treated per the preregistered policy; pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) would be excluded from the primary analysis and included in sensitivity analyses.

Model, adapter, and verifier contract. Execution used the declared model gpt‑5‑mini and the adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 under shared_initial_candidate semantics; the deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract exactly one initial generation was produced per task and reused across both arms; only validator failures of that shared candidate or a subsequent validator‑triggered repair could create discordant paired outcomes.

Scoring and analysis. Final outcomes were binary (safe vs unsafe) determined by deterministic emulator execution and semantic invariant checks encoded in the verifier. The primary analysis used an exact paired test: McNemar two‑sided for discordant pairs and a paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) for the paired difference. Secondary planned measures included median repair counts per arm and model‑call budgets. The analysis plan and all parameters were frozen in the preregistration.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run adhered to the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Hosted model call events = 240 and model_calls_used = 240, consistent with the shared_initial_candidate contract (one shared initial generation per task). No infra failures occurred and no preregistered exclusions were applied.

Primary outcomes and exact statistics. Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Observed counts: baseline_safe = 240/240 (baseline_unsafe = 0), guarded_safe = 240/240 (guarded_unsafe = 0). Paired contingency: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These outputs follow directly from the preregistered paired analysis executor and the observed contingency counts.

Validator activity and repair utilization. No validator‑triggered repairs were applied; repair_attempts = 0 across paired episodes. Representative validator traces record validation outcomes, required command counts, and difficulty labels for tasks; in every case the deterministic verifier reported the shared initial candidate as valid, so the guarded pipeline did not perform repairs and the final guarded configuration matched the baseline.

Subgroup slices. The in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, and adversarial strata each show identical safe outcomes under both arms (all zeros for unsafe applies); subgroup contingency slices are therefore degenerate and give the same paired difference of 0.00. Planned sensitivity channels for 'possible false‑safe' or infra treatment were unused because no such items occurred.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics mechanically ties the paired contrast to the fate of a single shared LLM candidate per task: only validator failures of that candidate (or an invoked repair) can produce discordant paired outcomes. In this execution every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs were triggered; consequently the guarded arm could not differ from baseline and the paired contrast was necessarily degenerate. This mechanistic explanation is supported by the execution accounting (one shared generation per task) and validator pass records.

Design tradeoffs and implications. Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces model calls and yields an exact pairing of generator output between arms, which is desirable for isolating post‑generation effects. However, it also makes the primary paired estimand uninformative when generated candidates rarely fail validation. To measure verifier causal impact in practice, experimenters should consider at least one of the following (artifact‑grounded recommendations): (A) allow independent initial generations per arm so generator variability can reveal verifier impact; (B) increase adversarial strength or introduce controlled generator perturbations to raise the initial failure rate; or (C) increase repair budget (permit multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair behavior to exercise the repair mechanism. These options follow directly from the observed zero repair usage and identical shared candidates across arms.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract is an explicit design choice that constrains causal interpretation; the contract and its runtime adherence were preregistered and observed. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encodes a finite set of semantic checks; although validator traces record observed touched fields and violation codes, unmodeled semantic fault classes may exist. External validity: the task corpus is an emulation‑grounded synthetic benchmark; extrapolation to production, multi‑vendor deployments and operator workflows is limited. Conclusion validity: the realized baseline unsafe_rate = 0 prevents detection of verifier benefit under the chosen design; power calculations contingent on a nonzero baseline failure rate would be required for informative hypothesis tests.

Practical recommendations for future GVR evaluations. (1) Choose generation semantics aligned with the causal effect you intend to measure: if verifier benefit is the estimand, permit generator variability between arms or intentionally raise the initial failure rate. (2) Instrument and allow richer repair protocols (multiple iterations and explicit repair traces) to study repair search behavior. (3) Harden adversary protocols (adaptive adversaries) if robustness under attack is a target. (4) Expand verifier coverage and cross‑check validator PASS against emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe behavior. These recommendations are practical and directly traceable to the observed execution artifacts and analysis.
sections.conclusion: We performed a fully preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline using declared model gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic verifier. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe), yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). This degenerate result is an artifact of the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with high validator pass rates: because the guarded arm could only differ from baseline via validator failures of the shared candidate or repair actions—and neither occurred—the paired contrast contains no discordant pairs. We present this artifact‑grounded account to clarify the causal interpretation of the executed estimand, and we give concrete experimental design recommendations for future work that seeks an informative estimate of verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial probes.

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model "gpt-5-mini" via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; the guarded pipeline employed deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). The initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Prior to the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial prompt; all literature review, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. The registered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one shared initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract paired divergences could arise only if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Execution artifacts (archived manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis outputs) exist in the study bundle for reproducibility. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across other models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite check set; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
